title: New York Times Prohibits Photographers From Using Photoshop 2027
summary: New York Times prohibits photographers from using Photoshop 2027 over AI features
detailed: The New York Times emailed freelance photographers and contributors prohibiting them from using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0) on assignment.
The ban stems from new generative AI features in Photoshop 2027 that are integrated in ways that may not be apparent to users or metadata systems.
The publication mandates that published photos remain accurate depictions of real events without unannounced AI modifications, additions, or object removals.
This matters as it highlights the friction between heavy native generative AI integration in creative software and journalistic integrity standards.
sentences: The latest version of Adobe Photoshop, Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0), added many AI-powered photo-editing features.
Not all photographers are thrilled about the increasingly heavy focus on generative AI inside Photoshop, and photojournalists are taking note, too.
As The Verge reports, The New York Times sent an email to freelance photographers and contributors warning them against using Adobe Photoshop 2027.

The email, which was shared on social media, specifically cites features inside Photoshop that use generative AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.”
The Times ‘ worries about Photoshop 28.0.0 are more about a perceived lack of clarity surrounding the application’s photo-editing features than the presence of AI itself.
Photoshop has included generative AI in many tools for years, including Generative Remove and Generative Expand.
The latest release uses generative AI for even more tasks, such as relighting and restyling photos.
New York Times photojournalists and freelance contributors cannot use generative AI on their photos.
In fact, as the publication’s ethics standards outline, all published photos must be accurate depictions of real events.
This means no people or objects can be added, rearranged, blurred, distorted, or removed.
It also means that cropping must be done carefully so as not to omit any relevant details in a scene.
Color can be adjusted, but only minimally and in service of accurately reproducing an event as it happened.
The Times adds that any use of AI, including generative AI, must be clearly disclosed to readers.
The organization has long embraced Adobe’s C2PA initiative as it relates to image provenance and metadata, and that is not changing.
What has changed, apparently, is how easy it is for a photographer to inadvertently use a feature inside Adobe Photoshop that relies on generative AI, which will then show up in the metadata.
This appears to be the primary concern for The New York Times, as it cannot work with photos that are labeled as AI-edited content.
“It has come to our attention that certain functions in Adobe Photoshop 2027 utilize generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users of the software.
At this time we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using this new version when working on assignment for The Times,” New York Times spokesperson Graham James tells PetaPixel.

To prevent these issues, all contributing photographers must entirely avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignments for The Times —an unprecedented blow to Photoshop’s already wavering reputation among professional photographers.
Fortunately, it is possible for users to install previous versions of Photoshop through the Creative Cloud app, although it’s not necessarily straightforward.
As of this writing, users can roll back to Photoshop 27.0, but no earlier.

Adobe’s insistence on publicizing its generative AI features, rather than the genuinely good and mostly inoffensive improvements made earlier this month to Adobe Camera Raw and Lightroom, has created quite a stir in the photography community.
The Times ‘s new policy will certainly not help Adobe’s PR problem with photographers.
PetaPixel reached out to Adobe for comment but did not hear back ahead of publication.
This story will be updated with any response.
